title: Hemolysis, Lipemia & Icterus (the HIL Index)

references.label: Standard clinical chemistry laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Tietz Fundamentals of Clinical Chemistry)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: Hemolysis (red cell rupture releasing intracellular contents), lipemia (excess lipid/turbidity), and icterus (elevated bilirubin giving a yellow tint) are three visible specimen characteristics that can interfere with chemistry and other testing — collectively assessed as the 'HIL index' on many analyzers.
explanation: Hemolysis can falsely elevate analytes concentrated inside red cells (e.g. potassium, LDH) and can also interfere optically with photometric assays. Lipemia scatters light and can interfere with photometric/turbidimetric measurements, and can dilute the aqueous phase of a sample in some assays. Icterus (elevated bilirubin) can interfere optically with assays read at overlapping wavelengths. Modern chemistry analyzers commonly measure H/I/L indices automatically and flag results that fall outside a validated interference threshold for a given assay; whether a specific H/I/L level actually invalidates a specific test depends on that test's own documented interference profile, not a single universal cutoff, so the analyzer/method's own interference table is the authoritative reference rather than a fixed number presented here.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any visible hemolysis automatically invalidates every test on that specimen — interference is analyte-specific; some tests are essentially unaffected by mild hemolysis while others (like potassium) are highly sensitive to it.
